# Specific detection of pigeon parvovirus with TaqMan real-time PCR technology

**Authors:** Cuiteng Chen; Chunhua Zhu; Shuyu Chen; Zhen Chen; Huanru Fu; YuYi Chen; Mengyan Zhang; Wenyu Zhang; Yu Huang; Longfei Cheng; Chunhe Wan

**Affiliations:** aInstitute of Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Medicine/Fujian Key Laboratory for Avian Disease Control and Prevention, Fujian Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Fuzhou 350013, China | bSchool of Life Sciences, Fujian Agriculture and Forestry University, Fuzhou 350002, China | cCollege of Animal Sciences, Fujian Agriculture and Forestry University, Fuzhou 350002, China

## Abstract

The viruses of the Parvoviridae family can infect both vertebrate and invertebrate animals. Recently, pigeon parvovirus (PiPV) was detected in the feces of wild urban pigeons. Owing to no specific detection platform for PiPV, studies on the epidemiology of PiPV are still a research gap. To achieve this goal, in this study, a TaqMan-based fluorescence quantitative PCR (TaqMan‒PCR) technique was established. The specific primers and probes used were designed on the basis of the NS gene characterization of PiPV downloaded from GenBank. After optimization, the established TaqMan‒PCR assay provides a sensitive, accurate, reliable and cost-effective platform for PiPV detection. We found that both YDPS and healthy birds can be found to have PiPV infection through field sample investigations, and we also investigated the presence of PiPV in Fujian, mainland China. Owing to the failure to propagate PiPV in embryos and cells, knowledge of PiPV replication mechanisms in birds still needs further study. In conclusion, a TaqMan-based fluorescence quantitative PCR method was developed, with the advantages of sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility. This method can be used for further epidemiological monitoring of PiPV infection.

## Introduction

According to the report of the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV), the family Parvoviridae includes 3 subfamilies (Densovirinae, Hamaparvovirinae, and Parvovirinae) and an unclassified genus (Metalloincertoparvovirus) (https://ictv.global/taxonomy). To date, there are 11 genera with 107 species, which have been detected in nearly all major vertebrates and both protosomes and deuterostome invertebrates (Pénzes et al., 2020; Cotmore et al., 2019).

Although members of the subfamily Parvoviridae differ in terms of viral proteins, their genome structures are highly consistent. The genome structure of parvovirus is linear single-stranded DNA, which is between 4-6 kb in size (Qiu et al., 2017; Streck et al., 2020). A typical genome generally contains two open reading frames (ORFs), encoding a non-structural protein (namely as NS) and capsid protein (namely as VP), with inverted terminal repeats (ITRs), which can fold into a hairpin structure on both sides of the genome. The presence of NSs, which are located on the left side, is critical for viral replication and assembly. Its N-terminal domain can bind to DNA and endonucleases, whereas its C-terminal domain functions as a helicase. The right ORF of VP plays a crucial role in determining pathogenicity and the host range (Gallinella et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2024b). The VP1 sequence comprises the entire VP2 (VP3) sequence but shares the same stop codon. A unique VP1 region (namely as VP1u) located in the unique N-terminus of VP1, which is essential for virus infectivity (Ros et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2017).

Parvovirus particles, such as chicken parvovirus (ChPV) and turkey parvovirus (TuPV), have been found in poultry worldwide with enteric disease syndromes since the 1980s (Dai et al., 2022; Kapgate et al., 2018). Recently, variants of parvoviruses have been discovered in different species of birds via viral metagenomic technology, leading to widely differing impacts on their hosts. Pigeon parvovirus (PiPV) was first found in the feces of wild urban pigeons (Columba livia) in Hongkong, China. Compared with chicken-origin parvoviruses and turkey-origin parvoviruses, PiPV contains a smaller middle ORF (155 aa), which is not similar to any other parvovirus genomic sequence. Amino acid sequence analysis revealed that PiPV NS (41 %) and VP (34 %) were associated with chicken parvovirus. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that PiPV may be included as a novel member of Aveparvovirus in the subfamily Parvovirinae (Phan et al., 2013).

Real-time PCR, which has the advantages of accuracy, reproducibility, low contamination risk and easy operation, has been widely used for the diagnosis of newly identified pathogens (Artika et al., 2022; Fu et al., 2024). To the best of our knowledge, no detection platform for PiPV was reported. Herein, we first develop a TaqMan real-time PCR (TaqMan‒PCR) assay for the detection of PiPV, our study lays foundation for further epidemiological surveillance studies of pigeon parvoviruses.

## Materials and methods

### Viruses

Pigeon-origin pathogens, including pigeon parvovirus (PiPV), avian influenza virus (AIV), pigeon paramyxovirus (PPMV), pigeon herpesvirus (PiHV), pigeon circovirus (PiCV), pigeon torque teno virus (PTTV), pigeon Megrivirus (PiMeV) pigeon poxvirus (PPoV), pigeon adenovirus (PiAdV), pigeon rotavirus (PiRV), and waterfowl-origin parvoviruses, such as goose parvovirus (GPV) and Muscovy duck parvovirus (MDPV), were also used as controls. These pathogens were all identified, isolated and preserved by the Institute of Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Medicine, Fujian Academy of Agricultural Sciences.

### Establishment of the TaqMan‒PCR assay

#### Specific primers and TaqMan probe design

Specific primers (PiPV-qF and PiPV-qR) and a TaqMan probe (PiPVProbe) (Table 1) were designed on the basis of the avian origin parvoviruses of Aveparvovirus in the subfamily Parvovirinae comparison and were verified via BLAST analysis. The designed primers were subsequently synthesized by Sangon Bioengineering Co., Ltd. #### Standard plasmid preparation

According to the NS gene sequence of the pigeon parvovirus HK8 strain (GenBank KC876004), the complete NS gene for pigeon parvovirus PiPVFJ01 was obtained via the primers in Table 1. The genomic DNA of the pigeon parvovirus PiPV-FJ01 strain was used as a template for PCR amplification. The reaction mixture was prepared according to the recommendations of TaKaRa Taq™ Version 2.0 plus dye (Takara Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Dalian, China). The PCR products were identified via 1.0 % agarose gel electrophoresis. The PCR-amplified target fragments were purified with a gel extraction kit (Omega Bio-Tek, Inc., USA) and inserted into the T-Vector pMD™19 vector (Takara Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). The recombinant plasmid was transformed into DH5a competent cells. Positive clones were selected for culture and subsequently extracted with a Plasmid Mini Kit I D6943 (Omega Bio-Tek, Inc., USA). The recombinant plasmids were sent to Sangon Biotech (Sangon Bioengineering Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) for Sanger sequencing.

The selected positive plasmids (namely, T-PiPV-NS2, amplified with PiPVNSF2 and PiPVNSR2) were evaluated via an ND-2000c spectrophotometer (NanoDrop2000, Wilmington, USA). The plasmid mass concentration was then converted to the plasmid copy number [number of copies = (amount × 6.02 × 1023)/(length × 1 × 109 × 660)], according to a previous study (Yun, et al., 2006). Then, 10-fold serial dilutions (5.40 × 109–5.40 × 10° copies/μL) were prepared via TE buffer (10 mmol/L Tris–HCl, 1 mmol/L EDTA). All aliquots of each dilution were stored at −80°C until use.

#### TaqMan‒PCR assay optimization

The T-PiPV-NS2-positive plasmid was used as a template, and a Premix Ex Taq™ (Probe qPCR) kit was used for TaqMan-PCR amplification. The primers, probe concentrations, and annealing temperatures were screened and optimized to determine the best reaction conditions for the method. Tenfold serial dilutions of T-PiPV-NS2 were used to generate the standard curve of the TaqMan‒PCR assay under the optimal reaction conditions. All of the reactions were conducted in triplicate. The plasmid copy number logarithm was plotted against the corresponding Ct values (cycle number threshold), and the standard curve of the TaqMan‒PCR assay was calculated (Zhang et al., 2023; Wan et al., 2018a; Chen et al., 2024a).

#### Specificity, LOD and repeatability detection

To evaluate specificity, PiPV, AIV, PPMV, PiHV, PiCV, PTTV, PiMeV, PPoV, PiAdV, PiRV, GPV, and MDPV DNA (or cDNA) were used as templates, and ddH2O was used as a negative control for the TaqMan‒PCR assay.

To evaluate the limit of detection (LOD), five selected T-PiPV-NS2-positive plasmids with concentrations ranging from 5.40 × 104 copies/μL to 5.40 × 10° copies/μL were used as templates, and ddH2O was used as a negative control for the TaqMan‒PCR assay.

To evaluate the repeatability, T-PiPV-NS2-positive plasmids with concentrations of 5.40 × 107 copies/μL, 5.40 × 105 copies/μL, and 5.40 × 103 copies/μL were selected for the TaqMan‒PCR assay. Three experiments were repeated within and between groups on the above samples. The coefficient of variation (CV) within and between groups was calculated via statistical methods based on Ct values.

### Field sample analysis

To verify the developed TaqMan-PCR assay, 75 fecal samples from 15 different racing pigeon flocks from sick pigeons with the etiological agent of young pigeon disease syndrome (YPDS) and another 120 fecal samples from 24 different racing pigeon flocks from healthy pigeons were collected. Five fecal samples from each flock were pooled into one sample. These samples were homogenized with sterile PBS in a mortar and then centrifuged at 4,000 rpm for 15 min. Nucleic acid was extracted from the supernatant via an EasyPure® Stool Genomic DNA Kit (TransGen Biotech, Beijing, China) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Additionally, all samples were tested with the established TaqMan‒PCR assay in triplicate and independently.

### Virus isolation

The TaqMan‒PCR positive samples were then used for virus isolation (Su et al., 2011). For SPF chicken embryos, the supernatants were filtered through a 0.2-µm syringe-driven filter and then inoculated into five 10-day SPF chicken embryos via the allantoic sac. For cell culture passage, MDCK, Vero and LMH cells were prepared and infected with supernatants. The cultures were incubated at 37 °C with 5 % CO2 and checked daily for cytopathic effects (CPEs). The developed TaqMan‒PCR assay was then used to determine whether the virus was successfully isolated.

## Results

### TaqMan-PCR

The optimal reaction mixture (20 μL) was determined by optimization and contained 10 μL of Premix Ex Taq (Probe qPCR) (2X), the primers PiPV-qF and PiPV-qF (0.5 μL), the probe PiPVProbe (0.8 μL), the DNA template (1 μL), and RNase-free ddH2O (20 μL). The reaction program was as follows: 95°C for 2 min; 40 cycles of 95°C for 5 s and 60°C for 20 s.

### Standard curve

The T-PiPV-NS2-positive plasmid was subjected to 10-fold serial dilutions (5.40 × 107 copies/μL - 5.40 × 10 2 copies/μL) for qPCR. The amplification efficiency (eff %) of the standard curve was 98 %, indicating high amplification efficiency (Fig. 1A). An R2 of 1.00 indicated a good correlation between the logarithmic value of the template amount and the Cq value at the different concentrations, and the slope of the standard curve was -3.42, with a Y-intercept of 39.56. ### Specificity, LOD and repeatability detection

For specificity evaluation, the data indicated that only PiPV-positive samples presented positive fluorescence signals, whereas positive fluorescence signals from the controls (including AIV, PPMV, PiHV, PiCV, PTTV, PiMeV, PPoV, PiAdV, PiRV, GPV, MDPV and ddH2O) were detected (Fig. 2A). For LOD evaluation, as shown in Fig. 2B, the limit of detection of the established TaqMan‒PCR assay was 54.0 copies/µL. ### Virus isolation

No SPF chicken embryos died during the 7-day observation, and no marked CPE was detected in MDCK, Vero or LMH cells. Moreover, no positive signal was detected via the TaqMan‒PCR assay. These data indicated that the isolation of PiPV was unsuccessful.

## Discussion

More than 60.0 % of emerging infectious diseases found in humans originate from various wildlife. Pigeons, especially racing pigeons and wild pigeons, have the ability to fly long distances, select the richest nutrients, and then return to the nesting region, which means that birds can not only be used for meat and eggs but also have potential for communication.

To date, avian influenza viruses, avian paramyxoviruses, pigeon paramyxovirus, pigeon herpesvirus, pigeon circovirus, pigeon torque teno virus, pigeon Megrivirus, pigeon poxvirus, pigeon adenovirus, and pigeon rotavirus have been found in pigeons (Jeong et al., 2021; Reid et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2016). These data allow birds to be recognized as natural reservoirs of multiple zoonotic viruses, which can lead to the emergence and re-emergence of zoonotic diseases for public health (Phan et al., 2013; Sahindokuyucu et al., 2022; Bodewes et al., 2018; Mia et al., 2022; Schmidt et al., 2021; Rubbenstroth et al., 2020). Recently, variants of parvoviruses have been discovered in different species of birds via viral metagenomic technology, leading to widely differing impacts on their hosts. Moreover, waterfowl-origin parvoviruses (GPVs and MDPVs) (Wan et al., 2018b; Wan et al., 2019), which belong to the subfamily Parvoviridae, were also used for specificity analysis.

Owing to its rapid analytical ability, sensitivity and specificity, convenient operation, and high throughput, quantitative real-time PCR technology has proven to be a very useful tool for the diagnosis of viral diseases, and is widely used for viruses detection worldwide. The TaqMan probe is an oligonucleotide labelled with a reporter fluorophore and a quenched fluorophore, which means that the unique advantages of the TaqMan-PCR are that it is more precise and sensitive (Artika et al., 2022). The developed TaqMan-PCR assay in this study were strongly correlated, and the amplification efficiency was high. Specificity validation revealed that only pigeon parvovirus presented positive fluorescence signals, with no signals from AIV, PPMV, PiHV, PiCV, PTTV, PiMeV, PPoV, PiAdV, PiRV, GPV, or MDPV. Sensitivity validation revealed that the minimum detectable copy number was 54.0 copies/µL. Repeatability validation revealed that the coefficient of variation for the repetitions within and between groups was less than 2.50 %. Our data showed that the established TaqMan‒PCR platform provides sensitive, accurate, reliable and cost-effective technology for detecting PiPV, which can be used for further epidemiological monitoring of PiPV.

The field sample analysis data revealed that PiPV-positive birds can be found in both YDPS and healthy birds, although the YPDS samples presented a relatively high positive ratio. These data indicate that PiPV may not be the main pathogen causing clinical symptoms of YPDS in racing pigeons. Owing to the failure to propagate PiPV via embryos and passage cells, studies on the pathogenesis mechanism of PiPV remain a major challenge, and the relationship between the infection of these pathogens and health needs further study.

In summary, we first developed a TaqMan-PCR platform with the advantages of sensitivity, specificity, and reproducibility for detecting PiPV. We presence PiPV infection in mainland China.
